title: Shelach: the fringes (Numbers 15:37–41)
hookLine: fringes on the corners of garments, to look upon and remember

cards: A string tied around a finger. A sticky note on the bathroom mirror. A hair tie on the wrong wrist so you don't forget to call your mom back.

Little physical things hold on to big intentions, the kind that slide off the mind by lunchtime. The Torah has one too, and it hangs off the corners of clothes, in synagogues and on ordinary sidewalks.
Watch someone at morning prayer gather a handful of white strings and press them to their lips.

teach.b: God tells Moses: speak to the children of Israel, and have them make fringes on the corners of their garments, through all their generations, with a thread of blue on each corner fringe. The fringe is called tzitzit.
And it's for this: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them". Look, remember, do: a chain from the eye to the hands.
Then the verse adds: don't go wandering after your own heart and your own eyes.
The Hebrew verb there is lo taturu, don't scout around, the same verb used for the scouts. Some readers hear that echo as the reason this paragraph closes the scouts' portion.
Rashi says the heart and eyes are the body's scouts: the eye sees, the heart wants, the body follows. The scouts let their eyes and fears lead them.
The fringes are a counter-scout, hanging right at your side. Rashi also counts the word.
The letters of tzitzit add up to six hundred; add the eight strings and five knots on each corner, and you get six hundred thirteen, the traditional number of the commandments.

Tradition says the blue came from a dye made from a sea creature, and that the knowledge of making it was lost, so most tzitzit are all white; some people today use a blue they believe has been recovered.
Some Jews wear tzitzit every day, under or over their shirts, and on a prayer shawl. And in traditional prayer this paragraph is said morning and evening, as the last part of the Shema.

how: Some Jews wear tzitzit daily on a four-cornered undergarment and on the tallit, the prayer shawl; at morning prayer, during the Shema, people gather the fringes and kiss them when the word tzitzit is said.

games.q: you're wearing tzitzit. by the verse, what are they for?
o: to show which tribe you're from.
to look upon, remember the commandments, and do them.
to keep the garment from fraying.
games.why: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them." eye, memory, hands.

practice: Find something you can tie, a thread, a shoelace, the drawstring on your hoodie, and choose one thing you want to remember: a person to call, a promise, a way you want to treat people.
Tie the knot slowly while you hold the thought, and let the knot hold the memory, so your mind doesn't have to grip it alone.
